questions.prompt: A farm can grow at most 100 tonnes of wheat or 25 tonnes of barley, at a constant rate. The manager says this year's crop of 80 tonnes of wheat and 10 tonnes of barley used every acre. Is that possible?
hints: What share of the land do 80 tonnes of wheat use?
Compare the barley that remaining share could grow with the 10 tonnes claimed.

acceptedIdeas: No, because that needs more land than it has
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because that needs more land than it has

choices.label: Yes, because the farm grew both crops this year
No, because that needs more land than it has
Yes, because the farm was working on its frontier

questions.onCorrect: Wheat uses 80% of the land, which leaves room for 25 × 0.2 = 5 tonnes of barley. Ten tonnes lies beyond the frontier, so the claim is impossible.

misconceptions.feedback: Growing both crops doesn't show the land was fully used. Work out how much barley the land left over after 80 tonnes of wheat could grow.
On the frontier, 80 tonnes of wheat leaves land for only 5 tonnes of barley. Ten tonnes lies beyond it.

questions.prompt: Maya turns down a £90 gig to go to a friend's wedding. Her friend says she lost nothing by coming, since the wedding was free. What do economists call the £90 Maya gave up?
hints: The wedding cost no money, so look for what going to it ruled out.
The word names the value of the best alternative you give up.

acceptedIdeas: opportunity cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The opportunity cost of going to the wedding. It was free to attend and still cost her the best alternative she gave up.

questions.onCorrect: The £90 is the opportunity cost of the wedding: no money changed hands, but a better use of the day was given up.

misconceptions.feedback: A sunk cost has already been paid and cannot be recovered. Maya never paid or received the £90. She gave it up, so it is a forgone gain and not a sunk cost.
The wedding had no price, which is why the friend thinks it was free. The term wanted names what was given up.

questions.prompt: In an hour Mira can code 4 web pages or write 8 reports, and Tom can code 2 pages or write 6 reports. Mira is quicker at both jobs. Why should Tom still write the reports?
hints: Price a report in pages for each of them.
Mira gives up half a page per report. What does Tom give up?

acceptedIdeas: A report costs him fewer pages than it costs Mira
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A report costs him fewer pages than it costs Mira

choices.label: He is quicker at writing reports than Mira
Mira's quickness at both jobs means she should do neither
A report costs him fewer pages than it costs Mira

questions.onCorrect: A report costs Tom 2 ÷ 6 = 1/3 of a page and costs Mira 4 ÷ 8 = 1/2 of a page. He gives up less, so he has the comparative advantage in reports even though Mira is faster at both.

misconceptions.feedback: Mira writes 8 reports an hour to Tom's 6, so he isn't quicker. What matters is what each gives up.
Being quicker at both says nothing about who gives up less. If Mira did all the work, the gains from swapping would be thrown away.

questions.prompt: Source A is Smith's example of a tailor and a shoemaker, and Source B is Ricardo's example of England and Portugal. What does Source B add to Source A?
hints: In Source A, who has an advantage over the neighbours?
In Source B, which country makes both goods with less labour, and does it still trade?

acceptedIdeas: A country can gain by importing a good it could make more cheaply itself
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A country can gain by importing a good it could make more cheaply itself

choices.label: Each trader should make only the goods it makes with the least labour of all
A country can gain by importing a good it could make more cheaply itself
Trade pays only when both sides could make a good equally cheaply

extracts.text: The tailor does not attempt to make his own shoes, but buys them of the shoemaker. The shoemaker does not attempt to make his own clothes, but employs a tailor.
extracts.who: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

extracts.text: To produce the wine in Portugal, might require only the labour of eighty men for one year, and to produce the cloth in the same country, might require the labour of ninety men for the same time. It would therefore be advantageous for her to export wine in exchange for cloth. This exchange might even take place, notwithstanding that the commodity imported by Portugal could be produced there with less labour than in England.
extracts.who: David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation

questions.onCorrect: Source B shows Portugal importing cloth even though it can make cloth with less labour than England. Portugal gives up more wine per cloth than England does, so it gains by making wine and buying cloth. Source A leaves that case out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reading of Source A that Source B rules out. Portugal makes cloth with less labour than England needs, 90 men against 100, and still buys it.
Source B has Portugal and England with different labour costs for both goods, and the difference in what each gives up is what makes the exchange pay.

questions.prompt: Ben gives up 1.5 loaves for every cake he bakes and Ana gives up 2, although Ana bakes more of everything in a day. What kind of advantage does Ben have in cakes?
hints: Ana bakes more of both goods, so it can't be the advantage of making more.
Think about whose cost of a cake, in loaves, is lower.

acceptedIdeas: comparative advantage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comparative advantage: he gives up fewer loaves per cake, even though Ana is quicker.

questions.onCorrect: Ben gives up fewer loaves per cake, which is a comparative advantage. Ana's speed at both goods is an absolute advantage, which is a different thing.

misconceptions.feedback: Absolute advantage means making more in the same time, and Ana does that. Ben's advantage comes from giving up less.
That is a business term for a firm's edge over rivals. The lesson's term compares what each producer gives up.

questions.prompt: A cake costs Ana 2 loaves to bake herself, and Ben will sell cakes at 1.75 loaves each. Ana buys 8 cakes from Ben instead of baking them. What does she gain?
hints: Price the 8 cakes at her own cost, then at Ben's price.
Compare 8 × 2 with 8 × 1.75.

acceptedIdeas: She saves 2 loaves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She saves 2 loaves

choices.label: She saves 14 loaves, the price of the cakes
She saves nothing, because she still pays for the cakes
She saves 2 loaves

questions.onCorrect: Baking 8 cakes would cost her 8 × 2 = 16 loaves, and buying costs 8 × 1.75 = 14, so she saves 2 loaves.

misconceptions.feedback: The 14 loaves is what she pays Ben. The saving is the difference between that and what baking would have cost her.
She pays, but less than baking would cost: 14 loaves against 16. Paying isn't the same as losing.

questions.prompt: The café's extra hours bring marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30. Wage and energy costs rise, and every hour's marginal cost goes up by £20 to £50, £55, £65, £70 and £80. What happens to the number of extra hours the café should open?
hints: Compare each hour's benefit with its new cost.
The third hour brings £55. What does it cost now?

acceptedIdeas: It falls, because the third hour no longer covers its cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, because the third hour no longer covers its cost

choices.label: It falls, because the third hour no longer covers its cost
It stays at three, since the benefits have not changed at all
It falls only if the café's average cost also rises

questions.onCorrect: The third hour brings £55 and now costs £65, so it loses £10. The first two hours still pay, so the café opens two extra hours instead of three.

misconceptions.feedback: Each hour is judged by its own benefit against its own cost. A higher cost can turn an hour that paid into one that doesn't.
Average cost doesn't decide it. The café compares each hour's benefit with that hour's cost.

questions.prompt: Over four extra hours the café's benefits average £63.75 an hour against costs of £40 an hour. A manager says the fourth hour must pay, since the average hour beats its cost. The fourth hour on its own brings £40 and costs £50. What is wrong with the manager's reasoning?
hints: The decision is about one more hour, not about the four together.
What does the fourth hour add to benefit, and what does it add to cost?

acceptedIdeas: The average hides that the fourth hour loses money
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The average hides that the fourth hour loses money

choices.label: Averages are never a reliable guide in any business
The average hides that the fourth hour loses money
The fourth hour's cost is already sunk and cannot be avoided

questions.onCorrect: The average includes the strong early hours. The fourth hour adds £40 and costs £50, so it lowers the café's net benefit by £10 however good the average looks.

misconceptions.feedback: Averages are fine as summaries. They are the wrong tool for deciding whether to add one more hour.
The £50 for the fourth hour hasn't been spent, so it can still be avoided, which means it counts.

questions.prompt: A theatre spent £5,000 on scenery that cannot be resold. Another week's run would bring £800 in ticket sales and cost £900 in staff and lighting. The manager wants to run it so that the scenery isn't wasted. What should she do?
hints: Which costs change depending on whether the week runs?
Compare £800 with £900 and leave the £5,000 out.

acceptedIdeas: Close it: the week loses £100 and the scenery is paid for anyway
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Close it: the week loses £100 and the scenery is paid for anyway

choices.label: Close it: the week loses £100 and the scenery is paid for anyway
Run it, because the scenery would otherwise earn nothing at all
Run it, because sales cover most of the week's costs anyway

questions.onCorrect: The week adds £800 and costs £900, so it loses £100. The scenery's £5,000 is the same whether she runs it or not, so it plays no part.

misconceptions.feedback: The £5,000 is gone whether or not the week runs, so it can't be earned back by a week that loses money.
Covering most of the costs still leaves a loss of £100, and that comparison is the only one that counts.

questions.prompt: A student values successive hours of revision at 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, and each hour costs her 25 points of other activities. How many hours should she revise?
hints: Compare each hour's value with its 25 points.
Stop before the first hour that is worth less than 25.

acceptedIdeas: Three hours, while each is worth more than it costs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three hours, while each is worth more than it costs

choices.label: Five hours, because every hour adds some value to her
Two hours, where the value drops below 40
Three hours, while each is worth more than it costs

questions.onCorrect: The third hour is worth 30 for a cost of 25, and the fourth is worth only 20, so she stops at three.

misconceptions.feedback: The fourth hour is worth 20 points and costs 25, so it loses 5. An hour pays only when its value exceeds its cost.
The third hour is worth 30 and costs 25, so it still adds 5. There is no reason to stop while an hour pays for itself.

questions.prompt: Demand for gig tickets is Qd = 100 − 2P, with P in pounds and Q in tickets a day. A promoter is thinking of raising the price by £5. What happens to the tickets she sells?
hints: Read the number in front of P in the equation.
It says how many tickets each £1 on the price removes.

acceptedIdeas: She sells 10 fewer tickets a day, two for each pound
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She sells 10 fewer tickets a day, two for each pound

choices.label: She sells 90 tickets a day, the quantity at a price of £5
She sells 5 fewer tickets a day, one for each pound
She sells 10 fewer tickets a day, two for each pound

questions.onCorrect: The equation loses 2 tickets for every £1 on the price, so a £5 rise loses 10 tickets a day, wherever the price starts.

misconceptions.feedback: Qd = 100 − 2 × 5 = 90 is the quantity demanded at a price of £5. The question is about a £5 rise from wherever the price is now.
The 2 in the equation means each pound removes 2 tickets, not 1.

questions.prompt: Demand for a good is Qd = 80 − 4P and supply is Qs = 8 + 2P. In what order do you find the price and quantity at which the market settles?
hints: You can't solve for a price until you have an equation to solve.
The check comes last, because it needs both the price and a quantity.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write down both equations first, then set Qd equal to Qs, solve for P, put P into one equation for Q, and put it into the other to check. Here 80 − 4P = 8 + 2P gives P = £12, and both equations give 32.

items: Write down the demand equation and the supply equation
Set the quantity demanded equal to the quantity supplied
Solve the resulting equation for the price
Put that price into one equation to find the quantity traded
Put it into the other equation to check that the quantity matches

questions.onCorrect: The equation comes from setting Qd equal to Qs, the price comes from solving it, and the quantity follows from the price. The second equation is a check that the arithmetic holds.

questions.prompt: The price of gig tickets is stuck at £25, above the equilibrium of £20. At £25 buyers want 50 tickets a day and sellers offer 80. What does the promoter see, and what pressure follows?
hints: Compare the quantity offered with the quantity wanted at £25.
Which side has more than the other wants?

acceptedIdeas: Unsold tickets, which push sellers to cut the price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Unsold tickets, which push sellers to cut the price

choices.label: Unsold tickets, which push sellers to cut the price
A shortage, which pushes the price up
Sold-out shows, which push sellers to offer more tickets

questions.onCorrect: Sellers offer 80 and buyers want 50, so 30 tickets a day go unsold. Sellers with tickets they can't sell tend to cut their price, which moves the market back towards £20.

misconceptions.feedback: A shortage means buyers want more than sellers offer, and here it is the other way round: 80 offered against 50 wanted.
At £25 only 50 of the 80 tickets can sell, so some shows won't sell out. More supply isn't what the numbers call for.

questions.prompt: Mill describes how the value of a commodity behaves. In the lesson's terms, what does the value adjust to reach?
hints: Mill's sentence says value brings 'the demand' to 'the supply'. What would make them level?
Which price in the lesson leaves neither a shortage nor a surplus?

acceptedIdeas: The price at which the quantity wanted equals the quantity offered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The price at which the quantity wanted equals the quantity offered

choices.label: The price at which sellers make the most profit
The price at which the quantity wanted equals the quantity offered
The price at which the market sells the most it could possibly make

extracts.text: We have seen that the value of a commodity always so adjusts itself as to bring the demand to the exact level of the supply. But all trade, either between nations or individuals, is an interchange of commodities, in which the things that they respectively have to sell constitute also their means of purchase: the supply brought by the one constitutes his demand for what is brought by the other.
extracts.who: John Stuart Mill, Principles of Political Economy

questions.onCorrect: Mill's phrase is the lesson's equilibrium: the price moves until the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. His second sentence adds that what traders sell is also what they buy with.

misconceptions.feedback: Mill says nothing about profit. He says value adjusts until demand matches supply, and the most profitable price needn't do that.
Mill's test is that demand equals supply. Selling the most possible would mean ignoring what buyers are willing to take.

questions.prompt: At a price of £8, buyers of a good want 48 units and sellers offer only 24. What is the 24-unit gap called?
hints: Which side of the market wants more than the other provides?
The word names the gap when demand outruns supply at the price.

acceptedIdeas: shortage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shortage: buyers want 48 units at that price and sellers offer 24.

questions.onCorrect: Buyers want 48 and sellers offer 24, so the shortage is 24 units, and in a free market the price would rise.

misconceptions.feedback: A surplus is the opposite gap, where sellers offer more than buyers want. Here buyers want more.
At equilibrium the two quantities are equal. These differ by 24 units.

questions.prompt: Tickets for a seller's shows sell out within minutes and a queue forms for any that come back. What is most likely true of her price?
hints: A queue means some buyers could not be served.
Compare the quantity wanted with the quantity offered at her price.

acceptedIdeas: It is below equilibrium, since buyers want more than she offers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is below equilibrium, since buyers want more than she offers

choices.label: It is below equilibrium, since buyers want more than she offers
It is above the equilibrium price, since the shows are popular
It is at the equilibrium price, since every ticket she offers sells

questions.onCorrect: Buyers want more than she offers, which is a shortage, so her price is below the one at which the plans match. A higher price would clear the queue.

misconceptions.feedback: Above equilibrium the seller has unsold tickets, not a queue. Popularity is why demand is high, and the price still sits too low.
At equilibrium buyers want exactly what is offered, so no queue forms. A queue of unserved buyers means more is wanted than offered.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys part of the coffee crop and the price of coffee rises. Which statement describes what happens on the market diagram?
hints: Which side of the market did the frost affect?
Once supply shifts, what does the higher price do to the quantity buyers choose?

acceptedIdeas: Supply shifts left, and buyers move up along their demand curve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Supply shifts left, and buyers move up along their demand curve

choices.label: Demand shifts left, because buyers want less when the price is higher
Supply shifts left, and buyers move up along their demand curve
Supply shifts left and demand shifts right, so the price rises

questions.onCorrect: The frost cuts what sellers offer at every price, so the supply curve shifts left. The price then rises and buyers move up along the demand curve they already had, so the quantity falls.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher price moves buyers along their demand curve and leaves the curve where it is. The frost changed the sellers' side.
Nothing in the frost changes what buyers want at each price, so demand stays where it was.

questions.prompt: Demand for coffee beans and supply of coffee beans each rise by 30 kg at every price. What happens to the equilibrium price?
hints: Check the old price: how much more do buyers want there, and how much more do sellers offer?
If both rise by 30 kg at the old price, do they still match?

acceptedIdeas: It is unchanged, since the two rises match
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is unchanged, since the two rises match

choices.label: It rises, since demand rose by 30 kg at every price
It falls, since supply rose by 30 kg at every price
It is unchanged, since the two rises match

questions.onCorrect: At the old price buyers want 30 kg more and sellers offer 30 kg more, so the two still match and the price stays put. The quantity traded rises by 30 kg. Had the shifts been different sizes, the price would have moved.

misconceptions.feedback: Supply rose by just as much, so the extra 30 kg wanted at the old price meets an extra 30 kg offered.
Demand rose by as much, so the extra supply at the old price is bought by the extra demand.

questions.prompt: A drought hits wheat farms. In what order do you work out what happens to the price and quantity of bread?
hints: You need a market on the page before you can say which curve moves.
The comparison needs both equilibria, so it comes last.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sketch the starting market first, then decide which curve the drought affects, then which way it moves, and compare the new equilibrium with the old. Here the drought raises the cost of making bread, so supply shifts left, and the price rises while the quantity falls.

items: Sketch the bread market's demand and supply curves and its starting equilibrium
Decide whether the drought changes demand, supply or both
Decide which way the affected curve moves
Compare the new equilibrium price and quantity with the starting ones

questions.onCorrect: The starting picture comes first, then the cause, then the direction, and the comparison at the end. A drought raises the cost of making bread, so supply shifts left, the price rises and the quantity falls.

questions.prompt: Six things happen in the market for coffee. Which is each: a shift of demand, a shift of supply, or a movement along a curve?
hints: Ask first whether the change is to coffee's own price.
If not, ask whether it describes the buyers or the sellers.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The incomes and the tea cases shift demand. The frost and the roasting machine shift supply. A rise in coffee's own price that cuts what buyers buy, and a fall in it that cuts what sellers offer, are movements along a curve.

items.label: Buyers' incomes rise and they want more coffee at every price
items.explanation: Incomes describe the buyers, so the whole demand curve moves.

items.label: A frost destroys part of the coffee crop
items.explanation: It changes what sellers can offer at every price, so the supply curve moves.

items.label: The price of coffee rises and buyers buy fewer cups
items.explanation: The good's own price is on the axis, so buyers slide along the demand curve they already have.

items.label: The price of tea, a substitute, falls and fewer people want coffee
items.explanation: Another good's price changes what buyers want at every coffee price, so demand shifts.

items.label: A new roasting machine cuts the cost of making each cup
items.explanation: Lower costs mean sellers offer more at every price, so supply shifts.

items.label: The price of coffee falls and sellers offer fewer cups
items.explanation: A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the supply curve.

questions.onCorrect: A change in the good's own price moves you along a curve. Anything else shifts the curve of the side it describes.

questions.prompt: Veblen argues that people buy some goods to show their wealth. A fashion label becomes the way to show it, and buyers want more of its handbags at every price. What happens on the demand diagram for the label's handbags?
hints: Is the bags' own price the thing that changed?
More wanted at every price is a change in which curve?

acceptedIdeas: The demand curve shifts right, because buyers' tastes have changed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The demand curve shifts right, because buyers' tastes have changed

choices.label: The demand curve shifts right, because buyers' tastes have changed
Buyers move down along the demand curve, because more bags are bought
The supply curve shifts right, because more bags are sold

extracts.text: In order to gain and to hold the esteem of men it is not sufficient merely to possess wealth or power. The wealth or power must be put in evidence, for esteem is awarded only on evidence. And not only does the evidence of wealth serve to impress one's importance on others and to keep their sense of his importance alive and alert, but it is of scarcely less use in building up and preserving one's self-complacency.
extracts.who: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class
extracts.kind: A book on the economics of social class

questions.onCorrect: When showing wealth makes the label more desirable, buyers want more of it at every price, so the demand curve shifts right. Taste is one of the causes that moves a curve.

misconceptions.feedback: A movement needs the bags' own price to change. More being bought at the same price means the curve has moved.
Sellers' plans haven't changed. The extra buying comes from buyers, who want the bags at each price.

questions.prompt: Museum demand is Qd = 200 − 10P, and the entry price is cut from £11 to £9. A trustee expects revenue to rise, and the manager expects it to stay the same. Who is right?
hints: Find the number of visits at each price from the demand equation.
Multiply each price by its number of visits.

acceptedIdeas: The manager, because revenue is £990 at both prices
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The manager, because revenue is £990 at both prices

choices.label: The manager, because revenue is £990 at both prices
The trustee, because more visitors always means more money
Neither, because revenue falls when each visitor pays £2 less

questions.onCorrect: Visits rise from 90 to 110, and revenue is 11 × 90 = £990 before and 9 × 110 = £990 after. Over this stretch quantity changes by about the same percentage as price, so the elasticity is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: More visitors bring more money only if the extra visits outweigh the lower price. Here visits rise from 90 to 110 and the entry price falls.
Each visitor does pay £2 less, but 20 more visit, so the two effects have to be compared.

questions.prompt: A bus company finds that, over the range of fares it is considering, the price elasticity of demand for its tickets is 3. It wants more revenue. What should it do?
hints: An elasticity of 3 compares two percentage changes.
If quantity changes by three times the percentage that price does, which change wins?

acceptedIdeas: Cut the fare, since ridership rises by a larger percentage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cut the fare, since ridership rises by a larger percentage

choices.label: Raise the fare, because each rider then pays more
Leave it alone, because elasticity does not affect revenue
Cut the fare, since ridership rises by a larger percentage

questions.onCorrect: An elasticity of 3 means quantity changes by three times the percentage that price changes, so a cut in the fare raises ridership by more than the fare falls and revenue rises.

misconceptions.feedback: With an elasticity of 3, ridership falls three times as fast in percentage terms as the fare rises, so the loss of riders outweighs the extra paid by each.
Elasticity is what decides the effect: above 1, a price cut raises revenue, and below 1 it lowers it.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy raises the price of a heart medicine by 10%, and sales fall by 2%. What word describes demand for the medicine?
hints: Compare the 2% fall in sales with the 10% rise in price.
The word describes demand that responds less than in proportion.

acceptedIdeas: inelastic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inelastic: quantity fell by a smaller percentage than price rose.

questions.onCorrect: Sales fell by 2% for a 10% rise, an elasticity of 0.2, so demand is inelastic and the price rise brings in more revenue.

misconceptions.feedback: Unit elastic demand would mean sales fell by the same percentage as the price rose, 10%. Here they fell by 2%.

questions.prompt: Gig tickets have demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20, so 60 tickets sell at £20 a day. A student says consumer surplus is the £1,200 that buyers spend. What is wrong with that?
hints: Surplus is a gain, so ask what the buyers got beyond what they paid.
Which part of the diagram sits between the demand curve and the price?

acceptedIdeas: Surplus is what buyers would pay above what they do pay
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Surplus is what buyers would pay above what they do pay

choices.label: Consumer surplus is the sellers' profit, not what buyers spend
Nothing, since surplus is the price times the quantity
Surplus is what buyers would pay above what they do pay

questions.onCorrect: Buyers spend £1,200, but consumer surplus is the value they get above what they pay: the triangle between the demand curve and the £20 price, which is £900.

misconceptions.feedback: Consumer surplus belongs to buyers. The sellers' gain is producer surplus, and neither is the money that changes hands.
Price times quantity, 20 × 60 = £1,200, is the money that changes hands. Surplus is the part of buyers' value above that.

questions.prompt: A rule caps gig-ticket sales at 40 a day, below the free-market 60. A council member says nobody is hurt, since the 40 tickets still sell at the same price. Who loses?
hints: Think about the 20 tickets that would have sold without the cap.
Would the buyers and sellers of those tickets have gained from the sale?

acceptedIdeas: Buyers and sellers who would have gained from those sales
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers and sellers who would have gained from those sales

choices.label: Buyers and sellers who would have gained from those sales
Only the sellers, who sell fewer tickets than before
Nobody, since the 40 tickets still sell at the same price

questions.onCorrect: For each blocked ticket the buyer would have paid more than the seller needed, and that gap is surplus nobody gets. The lost tickets form a triangle of surplus, which is the deadweight loss.

misconceptions.feedback: Buyers lose too: the 20 blocked tickets would have given them a gain. Both sides lose from a trade that doesn't happen.
The price of the 40 isn't the issue. The loss is the gain from the 20 tickets that no longer sell.

questions.prompt: Smith says we get our dinner from the butcher's interest in his own gain. Which idea from this lesson describes what the butcher gets from selling to us?
hints: Smith says the butcher acts from his own interest. What does he gain from a sale?
Which surplus belongs to sellers?

acceptedIdeas: Producer surplus, the gap between price and the least he would take
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Producer surplus, the gap between price and the least he would take

choices.label: Consumer surplus, the gap between what buyers would pay and the price
Producer surplus, the gap between price and the least he would take
Deadweight loss, the value of trades that do not happen

extracts.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages.
extracts.who: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

questions.onCorrect: The butcher sells when the price is above the least he would accept, and that gap is his producer surplus. It is his interest in that gain, and not kindness, that puts dinner on the table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the customer's gain. Smith is describing the seller's side of the sale.
Deadweight loss is the surplus lost when trades are blocked. Here the sale happens and the butcher gains from it.

questions.prompt: Six cases come from different markets. Which is each: consumer surplus, producer surplus or deadweight loss?
hints: Ask whether the sale happens.
If it does, ask whose gain it is, the buyer's or the seller's.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ticket buyer and the student have consumer surplus. The ticket seller and the baker have producer surplus. The two blocked trades, one by a cap and one by a tax, are deadweight loss.

items.label: A buyer who would pay £30 for a ticket buys it for £20
items.explanation: The gap between the most she would pay and what she pays is hers.

items.label: A seller who would accept £5 for a ticket sells it for £20
items.explanation: The gap between the price and the least he would accept is his.

items.label: A £28 buyer and a £15 seller would both gain from a sale that a cap on sales prevents
items.explanation: A trade both would have gained from does not happen, so that gain goes to no one.

items.label: A student pays £12 for a book she values at £18
items.explanation: She keeps the £6 between her value and the price.

items.label: A baker sells loaves for £2 each that she would have sold for £1.40
items.explanation: She keeps the 60p between the price and the least she would take.

items.label: A tax stops a £25 buyer from buying from a £22 seller
items.explanation: The £3 gain from that trade is lost to both sides, and the government collects nothing on it.

questions.onCorrect: Surplus is a gap between a value or cost and the price. When a sale happens the gap belongs to the buyer or the seller, and when a sale is blocked it belongs to no one.

questions.prompt: A £6 tax per ticket is collected from gig-ticket sellers. A reporter writes that the venues pay the tax, so ticket prices will not change. What does the supply and demand model say?
hints: With the tax, sellers keep less than the price buyers pay.
At the old price, would sellers still offer as many tickets?

acceptedIdeas: The price buyers pay rises, because venues pass some of the tax on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The price buyers pay rises, because venues pass some of the tax on

choices.label: The price buyers pay rises by the full £6, because sellers always pass a tax on
The price does not change, because the law names the venues
The price buyers pay rises, because venues pass some of the tax on

questions.onCorrect: The tax cuts what sellers keep, so they offer fewer tickets at each price paid, and the price buyers pay rises. In this market it goes from £20 to £24, so buyers bear £4 of the £6.

misconceptions.feedback: In this market the price buyers pay rises from £20 to £24, so buyers carry £4 and the venues £2. How much is passed on depends on how each side responds.
Whose name is on the form doesn't decide the burden. Venues will offer fewer tickets at the old price, which pushes the price up.

questions.prompt: A £5 tax is to be collected from sellers of a good. In what order do you work out how much of it buyers bear?
hints: You need a starting price to compare against before you add the tax.
The subtraction needs both prices, so it comes last.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Find the starting price, rewrite supply for the tax, solve again for the price buyers pay, and subtract the old price from it. The difference is the part of the £5 that buyers bear.

items: Solve the market without the tax to find the starting price
Replace P with P − 5 in the supply equation, since sellers keep the price less the tax
Set demand equal to the new supply and solve for the price buyers pay
Subtract the starting price from the new one

questions.onCorrect: The starting price comes first, the tax then enters through supply, and the second solution gives the price buyers pay. The rise between the two is the buyers' share of the tax.

questions.prompt: Demand for table salt is almost perfectly inelastic, and salt sellers can easily switch to making other products. A tax is collected from salt sellers. Who bears most of it?
hints: Which side is better able to walk away from the market?
The side that responds less bears more.

acceptedIdeas: Buyers, because they cannot cut back much
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers, because they cannot cut back much

choices.label: Sellers, because the law collects the tax from them
Both equally, because the tax is paid once on each sale
Buyers, because they cannot cut back much

questions.onCorrect: Buyers barely change what they buy when the price rises, while sellers can switch to other products, so the price buyers pay rises by nearly the whole tax.

misconceptions.feedback: Who pays the government doesn't decide who bears the burden. The side that can't easily change what it does carries more.
A tax is shared according to how each side responds. Equal shares would need equally responsive buyers and sellers.

questions.prompt: A paint market has demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20 from firms' own costs, so 60 drums sell at £20. Each drum also does £9 of damage to people nearby. A tax of £9 a drum is collected from the firms. What quantity does the market now reach?
hints: With the tax, firms keep P − 9 on each drum, so rewrite supply.
Set 100 − 2P equal to 4(P − 9) − 20 and solve for the price first.

acceptedIdeas: 48 drums, fewer than before
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 48 drums, fewer than before

choices.label: 48 drums, fewer than before
60 drums, since a tax only moves money around
51 drums, 9 fewer to match the tax

questions.onCorrect: Firms now keep P − 9, so supply is 4(P − 9) − 20. Setting it equal to 100 − 2P gives a price of £26, and 100 − 2 × 26 = 48 drums, the quantity that counts the damage.

misconceptions.feedback: The tax raises the firms' cost of each drum, so they offer fewer at every price. The market moves to a smaller quantity.
The tax is £9 a drum, a price, so it can't be subtracted from a quantity. The new quantity comes from solving the market again.

questions.prompt: In that paint market 60 drums are made where 48 would be efficient, and each drum does £9 of damage. The firms say the market is efficient, since every drum finds a buyer. What is the flaw in that argument?
hints: A drum is worth making when what buyers pay for it covers everything it costs.
Whose costs does the firms' supply curve leave out?

acceptedIdeas: Drums beyond 48 cost more, damage included, than buyers value them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Drums beyond 48 cost more, damage included, than buyers value them

choices.label: Buyers value the drums, so the damage should not count as a cost of making them
The damage makes buyers want fewer drums, so demand has shifted
Drums beyond 48 cost more, damage included, than buyers value them

questions.onCorrect: Each drum finds a buyer, but beyond 48 drums the firms' cost plus the £9 of damage exceeds what buyers would pay. Those 12 drums cost more than they are worth, which is the deadweight loss of £54.

misconceptions.feedback: The damage falls on other people, and it is a real cost even though neither buyers nor firms pay it.
People nearby bear the damage but they are not the buyers, so demand hasn't moved. The market ignores their cost.

questions.prompt: A government sets a price floor above the equilibrium price of a good. In what order do the effects follow?
hints: The price change comes before the changes in quantities.
The surplus is the gap between the two quantities, so it can't come before them.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The floor is set first, the higher price then changes what buyers and sellers plan, the gap between those plans is the surplus, and sales settle at the smaller quantity buyers want.

items: The government sets a minimum price above the equilibrium price
At the higher price, buyers want less and sellers offer more
The quantity offered exceeds the quantity wanted, so a surplus appears
Sales are limited to the quantity buyers want, and goods go unsold

questions.onCorrect: The floor changes the price, the price changes both sides' plans, and the mismatch between the plans leaves goods unsold. Sales are held to the quantity buyers want.

questions.prompt: A city caps rents below the market level, and supporters say it will help renters. Using the supply and demand model, what happens?
hints: At the capped rent, compare the flats wanted with the flats offered.
Which side of the market is cut by a lower price?

acceptedIdeas: Renters who find a flat pay less, but fewer flats are offered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Renters who find a flat pay less, but fewer flats are offered

choices.label: Every renter pays less, and the number of flats stays the same
Renters who find a flat pay less, but fewer flats are offered
Rents fall to the cap and more flats are offered to meet demand

questions.onCorrect: At the cap more people want flats than landlords offer, so a shortage appears. Some renters gain a cheaper flat, and others can't find one at all.

misconceptions.feedback: At the lower rent landlords move down their supply curve and offer fewer flats, so the quantity doesn't stay the same.
A lower price moves landlords down their supply curve, so fewer flats are offered, not more.

questions.prompt: A workshop's total cost is £50 at 0 units, £70 at 1, £85 at 2, £105 at 3 and £135 at 4. A customer offers £22 for a third unit. Should the workshop make it?
hints: What does the third unit add to the workshop's total cost?
Compare that extra cost with the £22 on offer.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, since the third unit adds £20 to cost and £22 to revenue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, since the third unit adds £20 to cost and £22 to revenue

choices.label: Yes, since the third unit adds £20 to cost and £22 to revenue
No, since the average cost of three units is £35, above £22
Yes, but only if £22 also covers a share of the £50 fixed cost

questions.onCorrect: Total cost rises from £85 to £105, so the third unit adds £20 and brings £22. It adds £2 of profit, whatever the average cost of the three units.

misconceptions.feedback: The average cost includes the £50 fixed cost, which is paid whether or not the third unit is made. The unit's own extra cost is what counts.
The fixed cost is the same with or without the unit, so no share of it needs covering to make the unit worth making.

questions.prompt: The market price falls to £16. The firm has TC = 100 + q², with a £100 fixed cost it cannot avoid, and MC = 2q. At its best output of 8 units it loses £36. If it shut down, it would lose the £100. What should it do in the short run?
hints: Which costs does the firm still pay if it shuts down?
Compare the loss from producing with the loss from stopping.

acceptedIdeas: Keep producing, since losing £36 beats losing £100
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep producing, since losing £36 beats losing £100

choices.label: Shut down, since it is making a loss
Keep producing, since losing £36 beats losing £100
Shut down, since the price is below average total cost

questions.onCorrect: At 8 units revenue is 16 × 8 = £128 against variable cost of £64, so it covers its variable cost with £64 left over for the fixed cost. That is why it loses £36 and not £100.

misconceptions.feedback: A loss isn't enough reason. Shutting down leaves the £100 fixed cost to pay, which is a bigger loss than £36.
The price is below average total cost, but the fixed part of that cost is owed either way. Only the costs the firm can avoid by stopping count.

questions.prompt: A bakery's costs fall into two kinds. Which is each of these: fixed or variable?
hints: Ask what happens to each cost if the bakery bakes twice as much tomorrow.
A cost that stays put is fixed.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rent, the oven loan and the insurance are fixed. The flour, the gas and the casual staff's wages are variable.

items.label: Monthly rent on the shop
items.explanation: It is the same whether the bakery bakes ten loaves or a thousand.

items.label: Flour used in the loaves
items.explanation: More loaves use more flour, so it rises with output.

items.label: Repayments on the loan for the ovens
items.explanation: The repayment is due whatever is baked.

items.label: Gas to run the ovens for each batch
items.explanation: Each extra batch burns more gas.

items.label: The year's insurance premium
items.explanation: It is paid once for the year, however much is baked.

items.label: Wages of casual staff paid for the hours they work
items.explanation: More baking needs more hours, so the wage bill follows output.

questions.onCorrect: A fixed cost stays the same as output changes, and a variable cost grows with it. Marginal cost comes only from the variable kind.

questions.prompt: A firm sells at the market price and wants the output that maximises its profit. In what order does it reason?
hints: You can't compare marginal revenue with marginal cost until you have both.
The shutdown check needs the output you have found.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The firm takes the price as the revenue from each extra unit, works out the cost of each extra unit, finds the output where the two are equal, and then checks that it should be producing at all rather than shutting down.

items: Take the market price, which is what each extra unit earns
Work out the marginal cost of each extra unit at every output
Find the output at which marginal cost equals the price
Check that at that output the price covers the costs the firm could avoid by stopping

questions.onCorrect: Revenue per extra unit and cost per extra unit come first, and they meet at the output where marginal cost equals price. The last check is whether the firm does better producing there than stopping.

questions.prompt: A manager says: our average cost is £18 and the price is £20, so every extra unit adds profit and we should keep expanding. The next unit would cost £24 to make. Is she right?
hints: A competitive firm's extra revenue from a unit is the price.
What does the next unit add to cost?

acceptedIdeas: No, since the next unit costs £24 and earns only £20
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since the next unit costs £24 and earns only £20

choices.label: No, since the next unit costs £24 and earns only £20
Yes, since the price is above the average cost of £18
Yes, since the fixed costs have already been paid

questions.onCorrect: The next unit adds £24 to cost and £20 to revenue, so making it lowers profit by £4, however the average looks. The firm should stop expanding where marginal cost reaches the price.

misconceptions.feedback: Average cost looks backwards over units already made. The next unit is judged by its own cost against its own revenue.
Fixed costs being paid doesn't make a unit worth making. The unit's own cost of £24 still exceeds the £20 it earns.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − Q, so its marginal revenue is MR = 100 − 2Q. At Q = 30 the price is £70. Which statement is right?
hints: Put Q = 30 into the marginal revenue equation.
Compare the answer with the £70 price.

acceptedIdeas: MR is £40, below the price, since every unit's price falls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: MR is £40, below the price, since every unit's price falls

choices.label: MR is £70, the price, as it would be for a competitive firm
MR is £40, below the price, since every unit's price falls
MR is £30, the quantity sold

questions.onCorrect: MR = 100 − 2 × 30 = £40, well below the £70 price, because to sell the next unit the monopolist must cut the price on all 30 it already sells.

misconceptions.feedback: A competitive firm sells at the market price however much it sells. A monopolist's price falls as it sells more, so its extra revenue is lower.
£30 is the quantity, which is in different units. Marginal revenue is pounds added per extra unit, and here it is 100 − 2 × 30 = £40.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 60 − 2Q and has a constant marginal cost of £12. In what order does it find the price to charge?
hints: Marginal revenue comes from the demand curve, so the demand curve comes first.
The price is read off demand, so it comes after the quantity is chosen.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write the demand curve first, derive marginal revenue from it as 60 − 4Q, set that equal to the £12 cost to get 12 units, and read the price off the demand curve, 60 − 24 = £36.

items: Write down the demand curve, with price in terms of quantity
Work out marginal revenue, which falls twice as fast as the price
Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and solve for the quantity
Put that quantity into the demand curve to read off the price

questions.onCorrect: The quantity comes from marginal revenue and marginal cost, and the price from demand at that quantity. Reading the price off marginal revenue instead would give the wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Demand is P = 100 − Q and marginal cost is a constant £20, and a monopolist sells 40 units. If the market were competitive, would more or fewer units sell?
hints: In competition, price equals marginal cost.
Set 100 − Q equal to £20 and solve for Q.

acceptedIdeas: More, 80 units, as competition prices at marginal cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More, 80 units, as competition prices at marginal cost

choices.label: The same 40, since demand and costs are the same
Fewer, since rival firms push up the cost of each unit
More, 80 units, as competition prices at marginal cost

questions.onCorrect: With price equal to marginal cost, 100 − Q = 20, so Q = 80, twice the monopolist's 40, at a price of £20 instead of £60.

misconceptions.feedback: Demand and costs are the same, but competition prices at marginal cost, whereas the monopolist sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
Marginal cost is a constant £20 in both cases. Competition brings the price down to it, which raises the quantity.

questions.prompt: Smith says the price of monopoly is 'the highest which can be got'. In the lesson's model, how does a monopolist choose its price?
hints: Does a monopolist want the highest possible price, or the highest profit?
Which two quantities does the lesson say a monopolist sets equal?

acceptedIdeas: It sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and charges what demand allows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and charges what demand allows

choices.label: It sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and charges what demand allows
It charges the most any single buyer would pay, and then sells to that buyer alone
It charges whatever it likes, since buyers have nowhere else to go for this good

extracts.text: The price of monopoly is upon every occasion the highest which can be got. The natural price, or the price of free competition, on the contrary, is the lowest which can be taken, not upon every occasion indeed, but for any considerable time together.
extracts.who: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

questions.onCorrect: The monopolist picks the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and charges the highest price buyers will pay for it. That is high compared with competition, but it is not the highest price anyone would ever pay.

misconceptions.feedback: That price would sell almost nothing. The monopolist wants the largest profit, and that comes from selling more at a lower price.
Buyers can still stop buying, and demand limits the price. The monopolist can choose a price, but it then sells only what demand allows at that price.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta both set Low in a one-off game, although High/High would pay each of them more. If they meet every year with no known end, what can change?
hints: What can a firm do next year about a rival's price cut this year?
Compare one year's gain from cutting with the later years' losses.

acceptedIdeas: Each firm can punish the other's Low next year, so High/High can hold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each firm can punish the other's Low next year, so High/High can hold

choices.label: The dominant strategy disappears, so both firms choose High in every year
Nothing, since Low is dominant every year and so High can never hold
Each firm can punish the other's Low next year, so High/High can hold

questions.onCorrect: A firm that cuts its price gains once, then meets a rival that copies it and the price war returns. If the later losses outweigh the gain, High/High can be sustained by the threat of punishment.

misconceptions.feedback: Low is still the better reply in any single year taken alone. What changes is that a cut now can be punished later.
Low is dominant in each single year, but a rival that copies your last move makes a cut today cost you later, which can outweigh the one-year gain.

questions.prompt: Smith expects tradesmen who meet to end up with 'some contrivance to raise prices'. Using the lesson's price-war game, why would such an agreement need watching after it is made?
hints: Suppose Beta keeps to the high price. What does Alpha earn by cutting?
Is High/High a pair of best responses?

acceptedIdeas: Each firm gains by cutting its price in secret while the other keeps the deal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each firm gains by cutting its price in secret while the other keeps the deal

choices.label: Each firm earns most when both keep the deal, so nobody breaks it
Each firm gains by cutting its price in secret while the other keeps the deal
Raising prices together is always a Nash equilibrium, so no one needs to watch

extracts.text: People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.
extracts.who: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

questions.onCorrect: Given a rival at the agreed high price, cutting pays more, so each firm is tempted to cheat. That is the prisoner's dilemma, and it is why price agreements need policing.

misconceptions.feedback: Both earn more under the deal than in a price war, but a firm that alone cuts its price earns more still, which is what makes the deal fragile.
In the price-war game High/High isn't an equilibrium, because each firm does better by switching to Low while the other holds High.

questions.prompt: Six descriptions come from different markets. Which structure does each one describe: perfect competition, monopoly or oligopoly?
hints: Ask how many sellers there are, and whether one seller's choice matters to the others.
Game theory applies where a few firms' choices affect each other.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The wheat farms and the seller who loses every customer on a rise are perfectly competitive. The ferry licence and the seller with no rivals are monopolies. The phone firms and the firms whose best price depends on rivals are an oligopoly.

items.label: Thousands of farms sell identical wheat, and each takes the market price
items.explanation: Each seller is too small to affect the price, so none has a strategy to choose.

items.label: One firm holds the only licence to run the ferry
items.explanation: With no rival, it faces the whole market demand curve.

items.label: Three firms supply most mobile phone contracts, and each watches the others' prices
items.explanation: A few firms each affect the others, so their choices form a game.

items.label: A seller who raises its price loses every customer to rivals
items.explanation: Identical goods and many sellers mean it must take the market price.

items.label: A seller can raise its price without losing every buyer, and has no rivals to match
items.explanation: It chooses a point on the demand curve, and no one else's choice enters.

items.label: Each firm's best price depends on what its rivals choose
items.explanation: That interdependence is what makes best responses and equilibria matter.

questions.onCorrect: Perfect competition has too many sellers for any one to matter, a monopoly has none to react to, and an oligopoly has a few that watch each other. Only the last is a strategic game.

flashcards.front: A film ticket costs £12 and a meal costs £6. You buy the ticket instead of the meal. What is the ticket's opportunity cost?
flashcards.back: Two meals, the best alternative the £12 could have bought.

acceptedIdeas: two meals
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two meals, the best alternative the £12 could have bought.

flashcards.front: Why is a production possibilities frontier usually bowed outward?
flashcards.back: Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit of one good costs more of the other than the one before.

acceptedIdeas: resources are not equally suited to both goods
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit of one good costs more of the other than the one before.

flashcards.front: A nurse is also the quickest typist in her ward. Why might she still hire a clerk to type?
flashcards.back: Her time is worth more in nursing, so typing costs her more of that than it costs the clerk. The clerk has the comparative advantage in typing.

acceptedIdeas: comparative advantage
acceptedAlternatives: the clerk has the comparative advantage
she gives up more by typing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her time is worth more in nursing, so typing costs her more of that than it costs the clerk. The clerk has the comparative advantage in typing.

flashcards.front: A cake costs Ana 2 loaves and Ben 1.5. Name a price in loaves per cake that suits both.
flashcards.back: Any price between 1.5 and 2, such as 1.75. Ana pays less than baking costs her and Ben receives more than it costs him.

acceptedIdeas: between 1.5 and 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Any price between 1.5 and 2, such as 1.75. Ana pays less than baking costs her and Ben receives more than it costs him.

flashcards.front: State the rule for deciding how much of an activity to do.
flashcards.back: Keep adding units while the marginal benefit of the next unit is at least its marginal cost, and stop when it falls below.

acceptedIdeas: at least its marginal cost
acceptedAlternatives: marginal benefit is at least marginal cost
benefit of the next unit against its cost
compare marginal benefit with marginal cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep adding units while the marginal benefit of the next unit is at least its marginal cost, and stop when it falls below.

flashcards.front: A firm has paid £1,000 for a licence it cannot sell on. Should the £1,000 count when it decides whether to open another day?
flashcards.back: No. It is sunk, the same whether the firm opens or not, so only costs the decision changes belong in the comparison.

acceptedIdeas: no
acceptedAlternatives: no it is a sunk cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. It is sunk, the same whether the firm opens or not, so only costs the decision changes belong in the comparison.

flashcards.front: What is true of the quantity wanted and the quantity offered at the equilibrium price?
flashcards.back: They are equal, so nobody who wants to trade at that price is turned away.

acceptedIdeas: they are equal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are equal, so nobody who wants to trade at that price is turned away.

flashcards.front: A rent is held below the equilibrium. Is there a shortage or a surplus of flats?
flashcards.back: A shortage: at the lower rent more people want flats than landlords offer.

acceptedIdeas: shortage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shortage: at the lower rent more people want flats than landlords offer.

flashcards.front: A heatwave raises both the price and the sales of ice cream. Does that break the law of demand?
flashcards.back: No. The heatwave shifts the demand curve right, so buyers want more at every price, and the higher price then moves them back up the new curve.

acceptedIdeas: no
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The heatwave shifts the demand curve right, so buyers want more at every price, and the higher price then moves them back up the new curve.

flashcards.front: Demand and supply both shift. Which of price and quantity can you name the direction of for certain, and why?
flashcards.back: It depends on the directions. If demand and supply both rise, the quantity certainly rises while the price could go either way, because the shifts push it in opposite directions.

acceptedIdeas: depends on the directions
acceptedAlternatives: one is certain and the other is not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It depends on the directions. If demand and supply both rise, the quantity certainly rises while the price could go either way, because the shifts push it in opposite directions.

flashcards.front: When does cutting a price raise a seller's revenue?
flashcards.back: When demand is elastic, because quantity then rises by a larger percentage than the price falls.

acceptedIdeas: when demand is elastic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: When demand is elastic, because quantity then rises by a larger percentage than the price falls.

flashcards.front: Why does the midpoint method divide each change by the average of the start and end values?
flashcards.back: So the percentage change, and the elasticity, come out the same whether the price is moving up or down between the two points.

acceptedIdeas: come out the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So the percentage change, and the elasticity, come out the same whether the price is moving up or down between the two points.

flashcards.front: What is consumer surplus?
flashcards.back: The gap between the most buyers would pay and the price they actually pay, added up over the units bought.

acceptedIdeas: the gap between the most buyers would pay and the price they actually pay
acceptedAlternatives: what buyers would pay less what they pay
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gap between the most buyers would pay and the price they actually pay, added up over the units bought.

flashcards.front: Why is total surplus largest at the equilibrium quantity?
flashcards.back: Every unit up to it is worth more to a buyer than it costs a seller, and every unit beyond it costs more than it is worth.

acceptedIdeas: worth more to a buyer than it costs a seller
acceptedAlternatives: benefit exceeds cost up to equilibrium
every trade that gains is made
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every unit up to it is worth more to a buyer than it costs a seller, and every unit beyond it costs more than it is worth.

flashcards.front: What is the deadweight loss of a tax?
flashcards.back: The surplus on the trades the tax prevents, which neither buyers, sellers nor the government gets.

acceptedIdeas: the surplus on the trades the tax prevents
acceptedAlternatives: value of trades that no longer happen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The surplus on the trades the tax prevents, which neither buyers, sellers nor the government gets.

flashcards.front: Does it matter by law whether the buyer or the seller sends a tax to the government?
flashcards.back: No. The burden is shared according to how strongly each side responds to price, whoever sends the money.

acceptedIdeas: no
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The burden is shared according to how strongly each side responds to price, whoever sends the money.

flashcards.front: What does a price ceiling set below the equilibrium price create?
flashcards.back: A shortage, because the quantity wanted at the lower price exceeds the quantity offered.

acceptedIdeas: a shortage
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shortage, because the quantity wanted at the lower price exceeds the quantity offered.

flashcards.front: Why does a market overproduce a good whose production harms bystanders?
flashcards.back: The firms' costs leave out the harm, so the price is too low and too much is made, until a tax equal to the harm makes them count it.

acceptedIdeas: leave out the harm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The firms' costs leave out the harm, so the price is too low and too much is made, until a tax equal to the harm makes them count it.

flashcards.front: At what output does a firm that takes the market price maximise profit?
flashcards.back: Where its marginal cost equals the price, because each unit before that earns more than it costs and each unit after earns less.

acceptedIdeas: marginal cost equals the price
acceptedAlternatives: where marginal cost equals the price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Where its marginal cost equals the price, because each unit before that earns more than it costs and each unit after earns less.

flashcards.front: In the short run, a firm's price is below its average total cost but above its average variable cost. Should it shut down?
flashcards.back: No. It covers its variable cost and has something left towards the fixed cost, which it owes either way, so it loses less by producing.

acceptedIdeas: no
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. It covers its variable cost and has something left towards the fixed cost, which it owes either way, so it loses less by producing.

flashcards.front: Why is a monopolist's marginal revenue below its price?
flashcards.back: To sell one more unit it must lower the price on every unit, so the extra unit adds its price less the loss on the units already selling.

acceptedIdeas: lower the price on every unit
acceptedAlternatives: selling more lowers the price on every unit
price cut applies to all units
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To sell one more unit it must lower the price on every unit, so the extra unit adds its price less the loss on the units already selling.

flashcards.front: Why does monopoly cause a deadweight loss?
flashcards.back: It sells less than the competitive quantity, so trades that buyers and sellers would both have gained from do not happen.

acceptedIdeas: sells less than the competitive quantity
acceptedAlternatives: trades that would have gained do not happen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It sells less than the competitive quantity, so trades that buyers and sellers would both have gained from do not happen.

flashcards.front: What is a Nash equilibrium?
flashcards.back: A pair of choices in which each player is making a best response to the other, so neither gains by switching alone.

acceptedIdeas: each player is making a best response
acceptedAlternatives: neither player gains by switching alone
no one wants to change their own choice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A pair of choices in which each player is making a best response to the other, so neither gains by switching alone.

flashcards.front: Why can cooperation survive in a repeated prisoner's dilemma when it cannot in a one-off game?
flashcards.back: A player who cheats can be punished in later rounds, and the later losses can outweigh the one-time gain.

acceptedIdeas: can be punished in later rounds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A player who cheats can be punished in later rounds, and the later losses can outweigh the one-time gain.
